Today: The ridge axis that was over the Inland NW on Thursday 
will begin to shift eastward into the Idaho Panhandle as a deep
low wobbles toward the WA Coast. This will allow an influx of 
mid and high level moisture to drift northward into the region 
bringing filtered sunshine. Temperatures will remain warm 
topping out in the mid to upper 90s with with some areas 
potentially reaching the century mark. The air mass will support
warmer temperatures than Thursday but the presence of high 
clouds does add a decent amount of uncertainty exactly how warm 
conditions will be. Winds will be light with a moderate amount 
of terrain influence. Areas which experience northeast to east 
winds could see periods of breezy conditions near 10 mph due to 
the alignment with the general winds as they begin to be 
influenced by the approaching low pressure system.

Overnight into Saturday night: The low continues to drift toward 
the coast overnight and into Western WA on Saturday. A weak 
impulse moving out ahead of the low will come through the region
bringing an increased risk for elevated showers or sprinkles. 
Some hi-res models indicate a small threat (5-10%) chance for a 
few lightning strikes but this comes with very low confidence 
due to 850-300mb CAPE only on the order of 50-100 J/kg and very 
weak forcing. HREF also advertises near zero probabilities for 
lightning overnight, a model that has done well through the 
course of the summer. HRRR on the other hand, has some threat as
do a few other hi-res models so it will be something to monitor
given its high based nature and little to no rainfall 
associated with it. 

As we head into Saturday, the weather becomes a bit more dynamic 
as stronger lift arrives. At this time, the way things are 
starting to evolve come in different waves. First will be the 
threat for showers and thunderstorms along the Cascades Saturday
morning with some activity lingering near the Canadian border 
in the afternoon. Second will be showers and thunderstorms 
developing over the Idaho Panhandle and extreme southeastern WA 
Saturday afternoon and continuing in different waves overnight. 
Both areas have the potential for isolated strong storms with 
the higher threat leaning toward the Idaho Panhandle given the 
activity aligning with peak heating. Gusty outflow winds, 
lightning and fire starts, and brief downpours of rain and hail 
will be a concern with an cells. 

In between these thunderstorm areas, the major concern will be 
critical fire weather conditions from gusty winds and hot, dry 
conditions. An index used for this is the hot, dry, windy index 
which is showing areas of the Columbia Basin well into the 95th 
percentile. There is reasonable agreement amongst the models for
a surface low to deepen over NE WA or close to the Canadian 
border as the low is drifting inland initially pulling south 
winds across the Western Basin and into the Okanogan Valley then
starting to spread eastward while shifting to the southwest as 
the low begins to track east and cooler air floods inland 
dragging a cold front through. Winds across the East Slopes will
largely follow the footprints of the terrain and come from the 
west/northwest. Strongest winds on Saturday look to setup across
the Western Columbia Basin and into the Okanogan Valley where 
sustained speeds will be closer to 20-25 mph with gusts of 30-35
mph. The Spokane Area and foothills of the northern mountains 
will be windy, but speeds look to be a few mph lighter with 
speeds of 15-20 mph and gusts to 30 mph. The strongest winds for
the Eastern Basin, Palouse, L-C Valley, and foothills of the 
Blue Mountains will arrive later in the day and into the evening
as the cold front presses through and would not rule out gusts 
close to 35 mph when this occurs. Overall, it looks to be a very
impactful day in regards to fire weather for new starts and 
wind driven fires. We will also need to watch for blowing dust 
on Saturday around Moses Lake, Ritzville, Wilbur, and Omak. 

While lightning may be limited across the northern mountains 
during the day as the winds are blowing, the low will move 
through northern WA and into southern BC Saturday night into 
Sunday. This will keep the threat for showers and thunderstorms 
going well into the evening and overnight hours while winds 
remain elevated region-wide. The main threat for thunderstorms 
on Sunday will be in the morning with the system departing to 
the east and breezy winds becoming the most impactful weather 
through the day while temperatures cool back into the 80s.

warming and drying trend. This is quickly interrupted by another
